subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, April 23, consideration of the motion of the Minister of Finance that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself again into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Ralston.
Hon. II. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce):	Mr. Speaker, first of all I
should like to extend to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) my congratulations upon the able manner in which he has discharged what is always a very difficult and onerous task. His was a clear and frank statement of the country's financial position without any attempt to minimize the difficulties or to evade the responsibilities inherent thereto. In his speech as the chief critic of the opposition, the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) discharged his duty in a manner which was no doubt entirely satisfactory to those with whom he is associated and for whom he spoke. However,
I do not think he will think it a discourtesy on my part if I refrain from following his lead in the form of my remarks. I assume the function of a critic is to criticize, and in that respect the hon. member undoubtedly discharged well his duty. I think on this occasion he excelled himself. But as I listened to his remarks it struck me that they were singularly lacking in any constructive feature. He most skilfully evaded all recognition of the very difficult circumstances in which this country in common with all other countries is placed or of the problems which face this country in common with others. This thought came to my mind: Can it be possible that the hon. gentleman and those with whom he is associated are unaware of the significant changes, both social and economic, which have come about in this and other countries during the past fifteen years? These changes are not merely due to the depression of the last three years; they have been reaching a degree of completion in recent years but they have been coming about for at least fifteen years.
The object of a budget is, first, to acquaint the country with the financial status of the country and, second, to survey affairs generally with regard to trade and other matters,

The Budget-Mr. Stevens
both internal and external. I have intimated already that in my opinion the Minister of Finance discharged his duty in a most admirable way. He was unbiased by his difficulties and courageously disclosed to the house the precise conditions. Of course, any minister that does that lays himself open to criticism here and there with regard to the details of his speech. But it was necessary that this be done and I think the minister has discharged his duty with credit to himself and to the house.
My purpose to-day is to invite consideration by the house of certain factors which vitally affect our trade and commerce, both internal and external, and which have resulted in a considerable rearrangement of modern business practices. This rearrangement has been almost revolutionary in its character and effect. Old shibboleths such as the law of supply and demand, buy that we may sell and tariff for revenue only will not extricate this or any other country from the embarrassing entanglements into which their trade has been drifting because of the operation of these new and potent factors.
First, let us look at Canada. As far as Canada is concerned, the most tragic and significant fact is the subnormal price of farm products and the consequent loss of purchasing power of the people in a very large section of the country. Some one will say, " Expand your foreign trade," but that is no answer. I would point out this one simple fact, that apart from wheat-I am speaking now of agricultural products-we consume within the bounds of Canada the major portion of the products of our farms. I shall run over a few. We consume something like 98i per cent of the butter produced in Canada, exporting and importing very small quantities. We consume 90 per cent of the bacon and 98 to 99 per cent of the beef produced in Canada. These are the most important but there are others. The fact remains that the major portion of our farm products are consumed in Canada and, therefore, it behooves the house to give a very careful study to whatever factors are now operating to contribute to the embarrassment of the producer and to the low prices which the consumer is now paying. As I have intimated, it is my intention to examine certain factors, both internal and external, which have a vital effect upon this and other questions pertaining to the trade, commerce and industry of this country.
There is a startling fact to which I should like to invite the attention of the house. Since the war Canada has passed through what is virtually an industrial and trade revolution. This has not occurred among the
workers but in the control and ownership ot the business organism of the country. The more I study this matter the more startling it becomes. Private ownership and personal supervision have been displaced to an almost unbelievable extent by a bond form of capital and corporate management. This applies to industrial and commercial distributing concerns, and it is difficult to estimate to what extent this change has affected the well being of those engaged in agriculture and industry. In order to demonstrate what I am referring to in these general remarks I shall give the house certain facts which, in my opinion, have a very significant bearing upon our affairs. The tendency to merge business under a limited control was prevalent in Canada and abroad before the war but it was checked by the war. Just as the war checked the extension of the merging of business under limited control, so did the depression of 1929. Whether or not that depression was due to that tendency I should not like to say but the fact is that for the time being it curbed the merging of business. In order that the house may get a proper perspective of this matter, which I consider to be of very grave importance, I should like to quote from a government report issued in 1913. This is a report on industrial mergers and over capitalization and I shall read some brief extracts from it in order that the house may be seized of the significance of the movement at that time and its consequences. I propose also to examine some factors with regard to external matters. This report of 1913 says:
Towards the close of the decade 1900-1910 a tendency to form amalgamations became marked among industrial enterprises in Canada. The tendency reached the proportions of a movement more or less general in 19091910; but it later almost completely subsided.
Then the report goes on to quote the Monetary Times, to the effect that in that period there were a great many mergers formed absorbing 248 companies, the aggregate capital of which was $456,000,000. This however is the significant part of the quotation :
The outstanding feature of the merger movement in Canada as above developed was its lack of success. Of the 56 amalgamations just mentioned, several met complete failure, several were saved only by drastic reorganizations, and several had to defer dividends on bonds and stock issues. Profits estimated on the "savings" above enumerated-
That is, the savings due to management and to other causes usually given as arguments in favour of mergers.
-in many cases did not materialize. Consolidation in itself, it was found, by no means
The Budget-Mr. Stevens

guarantees economies or larger profits as compared with the operation of individual plants. Many unexpected difficulties cropped up in the process of welding individual plants together.
I read that merely to indicate that there were before the country and before economists certain facts which I do not think were given very much credence or very much attention; otherwise we should perhaps have known better than to do some of the things we did subsequent to the war.
Let us turn to the period following the war. During the years from 1922 to 1929 there were formed in Canada no less than 120 mergers, involving over 500 separate companies. Of power and paper mergers there were 8, which took in 58 concerns. A biscuit merger absorbed 7 of the old companies; the Eastern Dairies absorbed 10 local companies; the Dairy Corporation of Canada took in 6 separate companies; 4 flour milling companies absorbed 48 bakeries; 1 paving corporation gobbled up 14 independent companies; 11 public utility corporations combined 46 local companies; General Steel Wares combined 5 companies, including such concerns as Me-Clarys, which for a generation had been a household term in this country, and Happy Thought. It is difficult to realize the effect that this has had on our national life. The social change resulting from this was most striking, because this is what ensued. Of the 500 companies which were thus merged into a much more limited number, the heads of these companies vanished as leaders in business. Some of them of course were carried into the merger and occupied positions of leadership; but by long odds the largest proportion of these independent leaders were eliminated from the business life of the country and no longer contributed either their experience or their guidance to its affairs.
I have also under my hand a statement-
I will not read it in detail-showing that a large number of these companies failed financially; in other words, they were not successful as mergers. So that from the economic standpoint there was no gain to the country so far as they were concerned. In reference to this matter I would quote some extracts from a book recently published by Mr. T. E. Gregory. Gold, Unemployment and Capitalism is the title of the book, and the author is recognized, I think, by a great many as a high authority on subjects of this kind. His words in reference to this tendency to merge or to form cartels, to which he also

refers, should warrant I think at least some attention. This is what Mr. Gregory says:
To have both planning and freedom, regulation and perfect elasticity of organization and technique is an impossibility. The difficulty of reconciling capitalism and planning may be judged by the mistakes committed in the last ten years in consequence of the enthusiastic acceptance by certain classes of business men in all countries of the doctrine of rationalization.	.
Further on he says:
What has caused so many rationalization projects to fail, that is, to disappoint from the financial point of view, has been the neglect of the distinction between the technical optimum and the economic optimum; and neglect of this distinction is peculiarly liable to occur when the direction of economic enterprise passes out of the hands of those trained to think in terms of the market into those trained to think in terms of the process subsidiary to the output of a certain product or service.
Then he concludes:
The fact remains that the rationalized undertakings of the era 1922-29, with their enormous overhead investment, their centralization of initiative and authority, their greater ability to monopolize the market and to buy on the most favourable terms, have not shown themselves conspicuously more successful than the non-rationalized undertakings. They have lacked adaptability, and elasticity, and for my own part I believe we shall witness a less blind worship of size and authority and monopoly in business for some time to come, unless indeed the whole process of economic adjustment of scale of output to demand is to be permanently prevented by the intervention of the state.
In other words, he directs attention to the growing tendency towards the development of mergers and monopolies in business, and to the obvious failure of this effort. May I give a more striking illustration of the working-out of this tendency? I give this 'because it applies to the commonest of all foodstuffs, bread, and it does present to my mind, to the mind of every thoughtful person, and particularly, I fancy, to this house, subject for very careful consideration.
Six mill-controlled bakeries in Montreal, with an aggregate yearly capacity of 163 million pounds of bread, can supply four-fifths of the bread sold throughout the whole province of Quebec. The total of all bread sold in Montreal alone is some 88 million pounds. In other words, these six controlled bakeries could supply 80 per cent of all the bread required in the province of Quebec. The significant fact is that in Montreal there are 126 bakeries and in the province of Quebec 887. Yet these six have the capacity to control 80 per cent of the supply of the whole province.

The Budget-Mr. Stevens
Take Toronto. Six of Toronto's seven mill-controlled bakeries report a capacity of 202 million pounds. The total consumption in Ontario is 403 million pounds; in other words, these six bakeries in Toronto could supply half the total bread consumed in Ontario. And yet there arc 235 bakeries in Toronto and 1,111 bakeries in Ontario.
In Winnipeg we have this situation. Three mill-controlled bakeries have a capacity-77 million pounds-to supply the whole province, for the estimated annual provincial consumption is around 57 million pounds. Yet in Manitoba there are 57 bakeries in Winnipeg while in the whole province there are 136.
In Vancouver there are four mill-controlled bakeries with an estimated capacity of 50 million pounds, whereas the total consumption for the whole province of British Columbia is 58 million pounds. Yet. there are 99 (bakeries in Vancouver and 267 in the province.
This question of the development of huge commercial and industrial organizations, with Capacity far beyond the requirements of the community, and with the concentration of control of these industries in the hands of a comparatively small number, constitutes a problem which this country might well keep in mind when considering the policies to be adopted in dealing with these matters. Such is the story. In the light of those facts, very much abbreviated in the telling-and I have under my hand many more facts in support of my contention-can anyone say that our old methods of handling farm products will succeed? I submit this proposition to the house: in the face of the facts to which I have made reference wherein is justified the opposition to an attempt to give Canada marketing legislation which will enable the country, the producers and others interested to have at least some interest in the orderly marketing of their products? The leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) says: Let the government keep its hands off this business.

My right hon. friend has spent about two weeks in criticizing and
objecting to a bill which is designed, as I have intimated, to assist in overcoming the difficulties which have resulted from the concentration of business in a comparatively few hands.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend says: Let the Magna, Charta function anyway. He may question my other interpretation of his remarks, but Magna Charta will take care of all this.
Let us turn to the question of foreign trade. Are the old conditions of pre-war days operating now? The chief financial critic of the opposition (Mr. Ralston) says: Buy that you may sell. That sounds well; these old shibboleths, as I have said, sound well, but I ask him and the house: Buy from whom and how? From the cartels of Europe? Totally ignoring the change that has come over the organization of industry, business and commerce in Europe, totally disregarding the cartels that have grown up there in recent years, cartels which are international in character and which by their weight and influence very frequently largely direct the policies of government, they tell us that the only thing that is necessary is to buy so that you may sell. Let us examine the situation in regard to the cartels in Europe. In the first place the system so far as the internal operation of cartels is concerned is an old one. For instance, in Germany they have had cartels since, I think, 1874, but the cartel of Germany of pre-war days was one to regulate business within her own territory. These cartels, however, have now become international in scope. It is true that before the war there were a few international cartels; for instance, there was the carbide cartel, the rail cartel, that is concerning the production of steel rails, the incandescent cartel and the aluminum cartel, but it is since the postwar period that we see the development of the great cartels in Europe. These have been used as a means of readjusting the economic structure of Europe; that fact cannot be questioned. In the political, social and economic upheaval which has been occurring in Europe during the past fifteen years we find that the international cartels, understandings between groups of industry in different countries, have played and are playing a very important part. For example, let us take the Franco-German potash cartel. Both the German and French governments are interested in it and it very largely controls the supply of that commodity.
The Budget-Mr. Stevens

Quotas are fixed for producers and also for exporters. I shall cite a few more instances in a moment. In the light of the fact that these international cartels are operating by agreement among groups of an international character, it is not enough to come to parliament and say: The solution of all your difficulties is to buy so that you may sell, because we are dealing not only with governments, not only with conditions that arise out of the imposition of tariffs in Europe and elsewhere, but with a completely new business structure that did not exist before and is of a tremendously important and potent character.
Let us take, for example, the steel cartel. Germany takes 43 per cent; France, 32 per cent, Belgium and, I think, one or two other countries the balance. Let me illustrate my point now. Canada is anxious and desirous in every way of trading with Belgium. Belgium is anxious to trade with Canada. That therefore looks like a comparatively simple proposition, but when we come down to a study of the actualities, what do we find? We find that a great steel cartel which controls the output of steel in Belgium as well as in Germany and France, has indicated that the price of steel exported to Canada shall be at a certain figure, which figure has no relation to the cost of production. I ask the house: Is the government of Canada called upon to stand idly by and allow an international industrial cartel in Europe to ship steel into Canada at figures obviously unfair according to our law as applied since 1905 to all other countries regarding goods sold at prices below cost of production? We cannot do so and that is one of the problems that arise between countries when they attempt to make agreements or understandings.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How are you going to break that?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will follow me I shall try to elucidate this matter a little further. Under this cartel one dollar per ton is taken for the ordinary business affairs of the cartel, but should one member of it exceed its production quota, it is fined $4 a ton and out of the fund thus raised those who come under the quota are paid for any losses which they may incur. For instance, the German industrialists had, I think, to pay several million dollars into this fund. I am seeking, however, to emphasize the fact of the existence of these cartels.
Let me cite one or two others. There is the chemical cartel which has grown to proportions that I think were undreamed of before the war. It is still in existence. I am not

condemning cartels but I am inviting the house to take note of the fact of their existence just as I have invited the house to take note of the fact of the merger of companies in Canada as a new set-up in the structure of our business organizations. There is the rayon cartel, well known to be a strong international set-up, and the linoleum cartel. The copper cartel in 1928 and 1929 fixed a price of eighteen cents a pound and copper stood at that figure for two or three years. It is true that after the depression set in the price was broken, but the cartel is still in existence. Let us take lead and zinc. As regards zinc, Belgium, Holland, France, Germany, Poland, Great Britain, Spain and, I think in a sense Canada and the United States, are in this cartel. I remember not so very long ago that certain purchasers of lead, wanting to buy it in large quantities for a European country, were desirous of buying it in Canada. What did they find? The only place where they could buy that lead was in London from a certain firm which controls the export of lead to those countries. Why? Because of an international understanding among the countries of the world controlling the marketing of lead. It may be argued that the government of Canada should force, for instance, any Canadian producer to step out. But what would happen? Simply this; you would close up your lead mines, and the Canadian producer would have no opportunity of marketing his goods in any of these countries.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In that case could not the
government itself step in?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, I think not, where
you have a large export as you have in lead, copper and other minerals. What I do think is that the conditions that have caused the cartelization of industry and commerce in Europe suggest the need of an international conference to give special study to this subject. I might say that the League of Nations have already taken cognizance of it and made several reports. As a matter of fact it is declared in one of those reports that so influential and strong were those at the head of some of these cartels that the League of Nations themselves felt that they should not go any further than merely cite the facts. There is a very interesting document published by the United States Department of Commerce, written by Louis Domeratzky, on this whole subject of cartels. It is a most illuminating document. There are also some utterances by the League of Nations.
I have cited this matter of cartels for the purpose of impressing upon the house the

The Budget-Mr. Stevens
fact that there are new elements entering into the question of international trade that were not present formerly. But that is not all. We must now recognize-I have referred to this before, I shall merely mention it- that the question of war debts has resulted in inhibitions and impediments to trade in the form of tariffs and quotas; this is another factor that is beyond our control. The fact that certain countries of the world have been submerged in debt to other countries constitutes an inflexible and inexorable barrier against the importation of goods into that country except under certain conditions. It is just as inexorable as the law of gravity, there is no escape from it. It is senseless and useless for us to talk about moving trade in certain directions when as a matter of fact by reason of the financial condition and obligations of given countries it is impossible for those countries to open their doors to foreign trade except under certain conditions which must take cognizance of the weight of the debt and where it is owed. Yet, sir, there are those who still say that we should extend our markets. Here is another factor which I invite hon. gentlemen opposite to consider. In saying what I now say I am not attaching any blame to hon. gentlemen opposite, I am merely stating a fact. During the years that hon. gentlemen opposite were in office, and I think in perhaps one or two instances before their time, there were some twenty-three most-favoured-nation treaties entered into by this country. What does that mean? It means simply this, if we follow the advice of certain hon. gentlemen opposite and make a trade agreement with Spain or Italy or Greece or any country in Europe covering certain items to be admitted to this country, the moment that agreement is made it immediately and automatically applies to twenty-three other countries. So, sir. when we discuss with a country the question of barter, if you wish to use that term as it is so frequently used lately, as my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) said in rather picturesque language the other day, all that is required is to give a quid for a quo-I do not know what he meant by a quid, it suggests chewing tobacco. Give a quid, he says, for a quo. But when you give a country its quid, there are at once twenty-three other countries that can chew on that quid just the same as the one to which you give it. That is one of the problems with which we are faced. It is a question whether that kind of international agreement was wise or unwise, for the moment I am expressing no opinion on that. I know arguments can be advanced in favour of it. But
I say without hesitancy that in the light of the changed conditions, in the light of these other factors in Europe to which I have referred, this doctrine of the most favoured nation, which is embalmed in some twenty-three treaties, is a distinct impediment to the making of agreements with other countries, a grave difficulty.

There is another point to which I wish to refer briefly. Statements have been made about the balance of trade. My hon. friend the critic of the opposition dealt with this at considerable length. It is interesting to note that our periods of excessive borrowings synchronize with the periods of excess of imports over exports. Let us pause and examine that for a moment. Open your doors and allow goods to flow in, they say, the theory being that the moment you do that goods will flow out; and the golden age from 1901-2-3-4 to 1907 or 1908 is cited as proof and support for that doctrine. But turn up your trade returns for these years, turn up your financial balances and what do you find? You find that during the years when Canada did its heaviest borrowings abroad imports exceeded exports. And that must necessarily be; it is as I said a moment ago a law of economics. But what this parliament and the country is called upon to do is to pause and ask itself the question: How long can such a process go on? Obviously it can only go to a point where the borrowings and the interest incurred as a result thereof become a burden beyond the normal capacity of the country to bear.
Let us follow that a step further. This may be a platitude if you like, but nevertheless it is a mighty important law in economics of trade and commerce. A debtor country must necessarily export more than it imports or else it goes in the hole. A creditor country will almost invariably import more than it exports because it is thus that its debts are paid. Let me give the house some very significant figures. Great Britain is a creditor country and has been a creditor country for many years. I have the figures of its imports from 1913 to 1932 before me. We find that imports exceeded exports 'by huge sums every year. There is not a single year so far as I can see in this whole list in which British imports did not exceed exports. But it did not follow that Great Britain was in any sense suffering from that condition, because she was receiving payment for certain things. It was payment of interest, it was payment for services, particularly ship-

But a country like Canada, that is a debtor abroad, that owes huge sums and interest, has no opportunity to pay except in goods, or by further borrowings. Speaking on this same subject in 1925, when the right hon. gentleman sat on this side of the house, I pointed out that there comes a time when a country cannot go on borrowing any longer. That time arrived two or three years ago as far as Canada was concerned, because generally speaking the money markets of the world were closed to ordinary borrowings.

My own criticism of the statement, if I had one. would be that I do not think they allow a large enough item for the services abroad for Canada. But, sir, let me go back to where I was when my hon. friend interrupted me. A debtor country must have an excess of exports of commodities over imports. I distinguish very sharply there between the export of commodities as against a general balance of the country's business. It necessarily must have an excess of exports of commodities if it is to make good its balances and debts abroad. So, sir, I wish to make this point distinct and clear, that while it is quite competent for a borrowing country to have an unfavourable trade balance and still be sound financially and make good on its general year's trade or business, for a country such as Canada with its heavy obligations abroad, such as interest amounting to $275,000,000 and other services, it is essential that such a country have an excess of exports to some degree commensurate with the adverse balance which is indicated, or it must borrow heavily abroad and increase the public debt, as was done in the years from 1904 to 1913. That is the only alternative. I have pointed out to the house, and I wish to emphasize this now, that this country knows that it is not desirable, if it can be avoided, to add to the public debt merely for the purpose of balancing the exports and imports of this country. Take our exports of lumber to the United Kingdom. In 1925 we exported 235 million feet; in 1930 that dropped to 187 million feet; in 1934 it had risen to 595 million feet.
When we take newsprint we find that there was a sharp increase in our exports between 1925 and 1930; and our export now is again increasing. Our average export in the last three years amounted to 39,600,000 hundredweight as against an average for the previous five years of 37,400,000 hundredweight. In drafting the legislation setting up this board, every reasonable precaution was taken to anticipate all the requirements essential to the free and untrammelled operation of the board, but with the many conflicting interests involved in matters pertaining to tariffs, it could not be expected that questions would not be raised as to jurisdiction or powers of the board. Such an instance occurred in connection with what is known as the jute twine case which was cited by the chief critic of the opposition. This was not a question as to whether or not the government would accept decisions of the board, it was definitely a question of jurisdiction of the board in making a decision in the form in which it was made. The matter went to appeal to the governor general in council, which was within the rights of the appellant, and it was decided to refer the point of law to the supreme court for a decision. It was a verjr difficult and considerably involved point and obviously some time would have to elapse during the period of consideration of the matter. There was no undue delay as the matter is now before the supreme court and it is entirely out of place to make it a subject of controversy on the floor of this house. Giving my own personal views, I have no hesitancy in saying that we have done everything we can faithfully to carry out the terms of the United Kingdom agreement, not only as it relates to this particular matter but to all others therein. Wheat was then selling at Si .08 a bushel and in the month of March of this year it was selling at forty-one cents a bushel. The people believed those promises in 1930 and they elected this government for which the Minister of Trade and Commerce is an apologist this afternoon.
The government kept two of its promises; one of those was to call a special session of parliament and the other was to increase the tariff. Parliament met in September, 1930, and the tariff was increased enormously against other countries. My hon. friend now talks about our trade falling off. I will Ehow him in a few minutes why it has fallen off. At the special session of 1930 the tariff was increased against every other country in the world. Then the Prime Minister went to the imperial conference at London and asked the British people to impose a tax of ten per cent on their food in order to give Canada a preference in their market. We all remember what the leaders of British thought said then about the matter; if they adopted that, they would be on a slippery slope leading to the bottomless pit. The Prime Minister came back to Canada and went to the city of Regina still talking about obtaining markets for Canadian produce. I can hear him yet over the radio when he came to discuss the matter of Cana-lian wheat; he said: My fellow Canadians who are now within sound of my voice, just at this very minute Mr. Marler, Canadian ambassador to Japan-and he would not be there if my right hon. friend had had his way in 1928-is on his wa}' to China to enter into a treaty with that great nation for the sale of your Canadian wheat. How much wheat did we sell to China? We heard some talk i few years ago by the government that they would not permit the sale of 100,000 head of Canadian cattle to Russia because Russia was an ungodly country. Still it was all right in 1930 for the Prime Minister of Canada to send Mr. Marler to China to enter into a treaty with that country. Within my recollection and that of the oldest man in the house, we have been sending missionaries from Canada to China to christianize them. How much wheat have we sold to China as a result of Mr. Marler's visit? We have sold none, but the Argentine republic, according to this pamphlet

which I have in my hand, published by the Department of Trade and Commerce under the authority of the Minister himself, in March of this year sold 2,756,000 bushels to China.

Next came the second imperial conference and the British people were to impose a tax of six cents a bushel on wheat from nations outside the British commonwealth to give our wheat a preference in their market. What ever came out of that? Political effervescence number two! No wonder the right hon'. leader of the government said when speaking in London in December, 1932, in connection with the imperial conference agreements that they should be considered rather in the light of the hope they offered for the future than in present accomplishments. I recall one of the Proverbs that says, "Hope deferred maketh the heart sick." The hearts of the Canadian producers of wheat are sick at the present time.
Next we had the world conference to settle the matter of wheat, with some fifty nations present. Notwithstanding the fact that the

The Budget-Mr. McPhee
Prime Minister of this country had given a bonus of five cents a bushel to the western Canada wheat growers two years previously, he now says we have too much wheat in the world, and the idea is to cut down the acreage. Well, two thousand years ago the greatest man that ever trod this earth, speaking in Judea said, as recorded in St. John's gospel: "I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly." Now we have the spectacle of the Prime Minister of this country addressing the Young Canadians in Winnipeg and saying in effect, that is all wrong, what our blessed Lord and Saviour should have said was, I am come that they might have life and have it less abundantly. We now have before this house that monstrosity the marketing bill in connection with our agricultural produce, a cross between Russian soviet socialism as sponsored by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and a Mussolini dictatorship as sponsored by the right hon. leader of this government. In 1929, $1,388,000,000 in value of exports from Canada, and in 1934, $480,000,000 tells the tale as far as this government is concerned.
That is one side of the picture. Let us look at the other. As I said before, this government kept two of its promises: calling parliament together and increasing the tariff. Right after they increased the tariff in 1930, one of the leading government newspapers of Belgium, in January, 1931, published an editorial, which I want to put on Hansard to make the record complete:
Just previous to his departure for the imperial conference in London, Mr. Bennett brought down in the Canadian house a bill dealing with the tariff. The tariff changes which were immediately put into force were adopted by the Canadian parliament. It is of some interest to Belgium whose exchanges with Canada have favourably developed in the course of these last years, to examine the situation and to bring out somewhat the point. . . .
We learn, moreover, that Belgium is, with the exception of Great Britain, its best European customer in the purchasing of wheat, oats and barley, and ranks second or third of all Canada's clients in the purchasing of these products; that it absorbs almost the total Canadian output of zinc ore and the greater portion of that of asbestos. . . .
Belgium can therefore not remain indifferent to Mr. Bennett's projected legislation of a distinctly protective character, and making for a complete revision of the Canadian customs tariff. It surely would be hardly conceivable that she should continue to be one of the best customers of a country which deliberately closes its doors to her products.
. . . Canada is not the only country which produces wheat, oats, barley, asbestos and zinc
ore. There is no reason why Belgium should not supply herself with these articles on markets which are more friendly to her productions.
That was the attitude of Belgium in January, 1931 following the increase of tariffs by. this government in the special session in September, 1930. And thirty-seven other nations followed the lead of Belgium in retaliatory measures against Canada. Let me put some of them on record. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) speaking at Guelph a few nights ago, said that no country had increased its tariff against Canada since the present government came into office, with the exception of duties levied on three small items by the Hoover administration in the United States. Let me put the facts on record. The fact is that thirty-seven nations retaliated against this country, among them are Esthonia, Siam, Poland, Germany, New Zealand, Mexico, Czechoslovakia, the Bahamas, Italy, France, the Argentine, Cuba, St. Vincent, St. Lucia, Colombia, India, Norway, China, Bolivia, Denmark, Uruguay, Greece, Switzerland, Belgium, the United States, the Netherlands, Jugoslavia, South Africa, Sweden and the Irish Free State. Let us examine some of these and learn the correctness of the statement made by 4he Minister of Justice that no country had increased its tariff against Canada since this government came into office.
Siam increased its tariff on tinned meats, fish, vegetables and fruits from 5 per cent to 20 per cent in February, 1931.
Esthonia increased its tariff on wheat, on March 26, 1931.
Poland increased its tariff against Canada on wheat, rye, oats, barley, rye flour, wheat flour, and rolled oats in March, 1931.
Germany increased its tariff against Canada on oats, hogs, fresh and frozen meat, and preserved meats, on April 30, 1931.
New Zealand increased its tariff against Canada on gum boots; newsprint and other paper; wire, including barbed wire, from free to 22J per cent on June 2, 1931, and on all other commodities from the preferential tariff to the general tariff.
Mexico increased its tariff on timber; aluminium wire and cable, bars, rods and sheets; pipes and tubing; butter, cheese, wheat and flour on May 3, 1931.
Czechoslovakia increased its duties on hogs in May, 1931.
The Bahamas increased the tariff on beans and peas, from 9 cents a bushel to 36 cents

Italy increased its duties against Canada on radios, and radio-electric and other materials, salmon and canned shellfish, three times in one year, on June 17, September 30, and October 3, 1931.
France increased its duties against Canada on canned salmon, hams, condensed milk, milk powder, cheese, rubber goods, boots and shoes, and belting, and all canned goods, four different times in the year 1931; on June 30, November 10, November 19, and December 10.
The Argentine increased its duties against Canadian wrapping paper; book, writing and wall paper; sewing machines; sardines; smoked herring in boxes and kegs; cheese; and gas cooking stoves on September 21, 1931.
Cuba increased its duties against Canadian knit goods and iron piping on September 21, 1931.
St. Vincent increased its duties against Canadian electrical apparatus on July 3, 1931.
St. Lucia increased its tariff against Canadian wheat flour on September 26, 1931.
Colombia increased its tariff from 4 to 8 ceqts per kilogram on wheat, and at varying rates on barley, oats, wheat flour, potatoes, canned vegetables, condensed milk, smoked and salted fish and rubber footwear on September 27, 1931.
India increased its duties against artificial silk piece goods, silk yarns and threads, and electric bulbs on September 30, 1931.

The United States, Switzerland, Jugoslavia and South Africa all increased their tariffs against Canada, South Africa four times

I understand that mj* hon. friend the Minister of Justice said there were only a few items on which there had been increases, but I have given the list which was compiled after a very careful and exhaustive study of the commercial intelligence journals covering 1930 and 1931.

While the Minister of Trade and Commerce was speaking I turned ever my file and found a letter that had been addressed to him from a merchant in my constituency, and if the minister or the government had taken any action on the matter brought up in that letter it would have helped the people of western Canada. I am sorry the minister is not now in his seat. This letter is written by a merchant in my home city, and is addressed to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It reads:
As a member of the Merchants Consolidated Limited I ^ am advised by them that the Welland Vale Manufacturing Company have refused to sell them harvest tools for the reason _ that they have two large wholesale houses in Winnipeg distributing for them in the west.
The Merchants Consolidated have a large number of members throughout the west, and they handle hardware, groceries, boots and shoes and dry goods. If the Welland Vale Company refuse to sell them, where are they going to buy harvest tools? On account of tariffs this company find it difficult to bring in tools from other countries.
Some relief- could have been given to the farmers of western Canada if this letter from the Yorkton merchant had been acted upon. The subject he mentioned was deserving of more consideration than harps or dried blood and the other items I have mentioned.
What is the solution, Mr. Speaker? The solution is a reasonable adjustment between debtor and creditor in this country, a reasonable reduction in the rate of interest to the farmers of the country and a tearing down of the iniquitous tariff walls that have been built up around Canada in the last three or four years. Perhaps I cannot do better than to put on record the words of a man better able to express himself than I can? Mr. Owen D. Young, of the United States, the author of the Young plan, and one who took a prominent part in the last presidential election in the United States as a supporter of Mr. Roosevelt. Here is one paragraph from an address that he delivered a few days before the election:
With the currencies abroad broken, with our own economic machinery threatened and endangered, with debts both domestic and foreign in every land crushing their people, it is time that liberal parties came into power to save conservatives from their own destruction, and to save the rest of us who are victims too. Not until then will our surplus cotton move from the plantations of the south-not until then will our surplus grain and' wheat move from the farms of the north-not until then will our surplus manufactures move from the factories of the country-and not until then will our surplus of labour and of commodities w'hich now economically crush us, disappear. It is the restoration of trade alone which holds not only the economic but the social salvation of the world.
[Mr. McPhee.l
To that doctrine we on this side of the house subscribe, and if it were adopted and put into practice then my hon. friend the Minister of Finance could very well look forward with renewed hope and courage and go forward with a firmer step towards the goal of better and happier days, but that will not come to pass until government of the people by the people and for the people shall again have its full measure of fruition in the legislative enactments of a Liberal government in Canada.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to add my congratulations to those that have been extended to the Minister of Finance for the budget he has presented to the House of Commons and the country. I think the people of Canada are particularly fortunate during these trying years of depression in having at the head of the Finance department a gentleman of the character and long experience and exceptional ability of the Minister of Finance.
The hon. member who preceded me (Mr. McPhee) devoted the greater part of his speech to a criticism of the government because they had not', so he claimed, opened foreign channels of trade, and because certain markets had been closed against Canadian products. I think his speech was answered in its entiretj' before he made it by the speech delivered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), who showed very conclusively from the official records of Canadian trade that it was during the years hon. gentlemen opposite were in power that foreign markets were lost to a very great extent, and that so far as natural products from Canada were concerned many of the products of Canadian farms and forests were being exported to other countries in much larger quantities during the past year than when hon. gentlemen opposite were in power.
My hon. friend from Yorkton (Mr. McPhee) referred to a few countries that had raised their duties against Canadian products, but the great majority of the products he mentioned are not natural products at all. Fie said that Italy had increased her duties against radios and radio parts. But those are not produced on the farms in Canada. He said that Cuba had raised her duties against knit goods and iron piping, and that India had raised her duties against artificial knit goods, and so on. Nearly all the items he mentioned were manufactured articles, not natural products at all, on which duties had been imposed by other countries. He said that Norway had raised her duties against Cana-

The Budget-Mr. Shaver
dian timber, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce showed that last year the exports of timber from Canada had increased by a very large amount over 1930.
The Minister of Finance was able to paint a rather optimistic picture of Canada's position at the present time, and I think that it was entirely justified by the conditions that exist to-day. The fact that we had a total increase in trade last year of $132,000,000 over the preceding year; the fact that Canada leads the world in per capita export trade; the fact that we had an increase in manufacturing production and, in railway revenues, and a gradual upward trend in commodity prices, all help the people of Canada to realize that the dark clouds of depression are passing away and that brighter days are with us.
I shall not attempt to deal with the whole speech made by the hon. member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) as I believe it was answered very conclusively by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. However, there was one point he made in his speech to which I should like to refer. He moved an amendment couched in these words:
This house regrets that the proposals of the Minister of Finance give no indication of the intention of the government to abandon the policies of economic nationalism which have proved so disastrous to Canada's trade.
A little earlier in his speech, dealing with the reduction in the drawback which the government was introducing in the budget in connection with foreign coal used in Canada for certain purposes, he made this observation:
If it means that there is to be a further restriction with regard to competing American coal, then so far as I am concerned, coming as I do from Nova Scotia, I welcome it because if there is to be a policy of protection the natural product of Nova Scotia as well as of other provinces should be protected, particularly in view of the national interests which exist in connection with the preservation of the mines of that province.
The hon. gentleman believes in economic nationalism when it is applied to the coal industry in Nova Scotia but he is entirely opposed to it when it is applied to the textile industry in the county which I represent.
In his contribution to the budget debate, the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw) criticized severely the protection which had been given the textile industry and the implement industry in eastern Canada. But before he finished his speech he asked the government to give special consideration to the beet sugar industry which I assume is located in his own constituency or in his own part of the country. He asked that the
government should give freight protection and by implication asked for a subsidy to that industry, -because he quoted the subsidies which had been paid over a period of years by Great Britain. That hon. gentleman believes in a policy of economic nationalism as applied to the beet sugar industry in his own county, but he is entirely opposed to it when it is applied to the textile industry in my county.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) has condemned time and again the existing tariff protection enjoyed by the industries of eastern Canada, but he has a resolution on the order paper protesting against the use of oriental labour in the shipping on the Pacific coast. He asks that this employment should be confined entirely to Canadian white citizens. The hon. gentleman is quite satisfied to have protection against oriental labour but he is willing that we should permit goods to come in from oriental countries manufactured under living conditions which Canadian people should not be expected to adopt and which we would not want them to endure. He is quite willing to allow such goods to come into Canada to compete with the products of the textile and other industries in the county which I represent. And this attitude is to be found among Liberal members from one end of the country to the other. When hon. gentlemen of the Liberal opposition talk about economic nationalism they always apply it to an industry which exists in some other part of the country, but they are quite satisfied that industries in their own sections should receive protection, either by way of freight rates, subsidies or tariffs. They cannot be accused of believing in a policy of economic nationalism, but they give a very clear demonstration that they are devoted to a policy of economic sectionalism.
During the years it has been in office this government has rendered outstanding service to the Canadian people, but to no section of the people have they given better service than to the farmers. No government since confederation has rendered a more- extended service to the agricultural interests of our country than has the present government during the years it has been in office. The protection which has been given to agricultural products; the empire agreements, which were strenuously opposed by hon. gentlemen opposite, and the marketing bill, one of the most forward looking and progressive pieces of legislation ever introduced into the parliament of Canada, have all been opposed by hon. gentlemen opposite. The best evidence that the empire agreements have been of
The Budget-Mr. Shaver

benefit to Canada is the fact that our exports to Great Britain last year increased twenty per cent over the preceding year, while we had much larger exports to other parts of the empire. In my opinion if the marketing act is to be a success it is absolutely necessary that the government administering the act must be one which believes in and practices the principle of protection. If we do not have a protected market; if our market is liable to invasion by agricultural products from foreign countries being dumped into Canada, the work of the marketing board will be rendered very difficult indeed.
There are two particular products produced in large quantities in the part of the country which I represent, and, as I have pointed out, the tariff on these two commodities has put millions of dollars into the pockets of Canadian farmers. I refer to butter and eggs. Hon. gentlemen know that during the years the Liberal party was in power our markets were flooded continually with butter from New Zealand. There was always a spread running from 6 to 10 cents per pound between the Montreal and New York prices, the New York prices being the higher. At that time our prices kept down quite closely to the London prices. In 1933 when butter was receiving the protection to which it was entitled, the average price in New York was 23-7 per pound; in Montreal, 21 cents a pound and in London, 16-8 per pound. Without protection I have no doubt that the Montreal price would have approximated very closely the London price, making a difference of at least 5 cents per pound in what the Canadian farmer would have received. We all know that during the winter months the price has been much higher in Montreal than it was in New York, and from 11 to 13 cents per pound higher than it was in London. In January the price in Montreal was 25-2 cents per pound, in London, 14-4 cents per pound, and New York, 20 cents per pound. In February the price in Montreal was 27-8 cents; in London, 15 cents and in New York 25-8 cents. In March the price in Montreal was 29-5 cents, in London, 16-2 cents and in New York, 26-5 cents. The only hon. member who has attempted to explain away these facts is the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Bertrand). During an address which he gave recently in the house he stated that the farmer of eastern Canada was not assisted because he produced very little butter during the winter. I wonder if the hon. gentleman took pains to find out how much butter was actually produced? I did, and I found that in December, January, February and March the farmers of Canada produced 33,000,000 pounds of

butter. Because of the tariff, the value of this butter was enhanced by at least 5 cents per pound, so that 81,650,000 was put into the pockets of the farmers of Canada.
The same is true with eggs. We all know that during the regime of hon. gentlemen opposite our market w'as flooded continually during the winter months with eggs from the United States. There was always a slump in prices during the winter months and the farmer never expected to get a reasonable price for his eggs during a period when it cost him the most to produce them. Because of a reasonable measure of protection and the initiative and energy of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir), who was instrumental last fall in having 2,000,000 dozen storage eggs shipped out of Canada to the British markets, thus taking them out of competition with fresh eggs during the winter months, we find that during the past winter the farmer has received exceptionally good prices for his eggs. When hon. gentlemen opposite were in power eggs were always imported into Canada by way of Chicago. On February 28 the top price in Chicago was 20 cents per dozen while the price in Montreal was 45 cents per dozen. On March 21 the top price in Chicago was 17 cents per dozen, while the price in Montreal was 25 cents.
The production of hogs is a large industry in eastern Ontario, the part of the province in which I live. The empire agreements, which were opposed in their entirety by hon. gentlemen opposite, have been of tremendous value in giving to the hog producers of Canada a larger share of the British market as well as better prices. We have only to compare the price in Chicago with the price in Montreal to see how the Canadian price has improved. On February 28 the price in Chicago for choice hogs was $4.80 per hundredweight, whereas in Montreal it was $10. On March 21 the price in Chicago was $4.40 and in Montreal $8.75. On April 28, just a few days ago, the top price in Chicago was $3.90 and in Montreal $9.10.
The only gentleman on the opposite side who attempted to explain away the facts was the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly), who not long ago, admitting that hogs had doubled in price in Canada as compared with the United States, brought forward this fantastic argument, that the United States did not produce bacon hogs but produced a short, thick, fat animal used chiefly in the production of lard. May I direct the attention of hon. gentlemen opposite to the fact that back in 1930, the last year they were in power, the United States, the country
which the hon. member for Willow Bunch [DOT]

The Budget-Mr. Shaver
tells us does not produce a bacon type hog, exported to the United Kingdom 145,472,302 pounds of bacon and hams while Canada exported in that year to the United Kingdom 13,011,400 pounds. The agreements with the United Kingdom came into effect in the fall of 1932, and if you compare the figures for 1930, of Canada's exports to the United Kingdom, with the figures for 1933, you will find that they had risen to 71,524,700, or five and one-half times what they were in 1930; whereas the exports of the United States to the United Kingdom had dropped to 73.355,663, or about half what they were in 1930.
That shows clearly the value of an assured market so far as that product is concerned, and it disposes effectually of the fantastic argument of my hon. friend, that the country to the south of us, with millions of farmers, does not produce bacon hogs.
With one product which the farms of eastern Canada produce, the marketing board, as so ably pointed out in his excellent speech the other evening by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Myers), will be able to do a great deal, and that is cheese. We are constantly on an export market with regard to cheese, because in 1933 we consumed only 27-6 of the cheese produced in Canada and exported 72-4 per cent. There has been a continually low price for cheese and it has been a difficult problem with many farmers in my own county. The fact is that we have been on an export market and I believe that the marketing board, by assisting in curing, storing and in giving a regulated supply to the British market, will have a considerable effect in helping the farmers in this very important industry.
I have reviewed very briefly a few of the agricultural items in which the farmers in my own county are interested. We admit that the prices of farm products have been low. But the prices of basic commodities throughout the world have been low, and Canada has shared in those low prices. It can be said without fear of contradiction however that the policy which this government has so far put into effect has been of great value in keeping prices at a better level as regards the commodities which I have mentioned than they would have been had not this policy been put into force. And while, as I sincerely believe, the farmers of my own county have benefited by the policy of the government, I am glad to be able to say that the Cornwall industries also have been assisted in that county by that policy.
In this connection I would read a paragraph or two from an editorial that appeared in the Cornwall Standard-Freeholder of Wednesday, February 14, 1934. It is headed "Cornwall is in the Limelight" and reads:
Believe it or not, the name of Cornwall is a magic word throughout Ontario to-day. Because of its rapid recovery from the effects of depression, Cornwall is occupying an enviable position among cities and towns of the province.
Wherever one goes, the comment is always the same-"You are from Cornwall ? Things are booming down your way, aren't they?"
It gives one a feeling of justifiable pride to hear admiring and sometimes envious remarks about Cornwall. We know that our industries are working at capacity, that employment today is actually greater than it was in the boom year of 1928, that relief is no longer necessary, that new factories are locating here, that Cornwall is experiencing a period of unparal-leded expansion while other cities and towns are just beginning to shake off the fetters of business stagnation.
There are various reasons for the prosperity of this large industrial town. One reason is that we have not all our industrial eggs in one basket. We have diversified industries and a splendid class of working people, both French and English, who for intelligence, industry and devotion to duty are unsurpassed by the working people of any section of Canada or on the North American continent. We have three railways and boat service located on the St. Lawrence, electric power at reasonable rates, and our street railway furnishes a switching service which is very efficient and helpful to various industries. We have also an efficient and active board of trade and city council. But notwithstanding all these factors, the most important, and the one that has contributed more than anything else to the success of industry in Cornwall, is the assistance which has been given by the tariff policy of the present government.
I have referred in this house on previous occasions to the additions that have been made to Courtauld's plant since this government came into power. This firm is a large manufacturer of rayon, and when this government came into power, in the short session of 1930, one of their first acts was to give this and various other industries in Canada the protection to which they were entitled, in order that they might maintain a large number of working people and pay them reasonable wages. This industry in 1930 was employing about 1,000 people. Immediately after the tariff policy of this government came into effect they began the construction of an addition to their plant and it
The Budget-Mr. Shaver

was finished during the following year at a cost of some $3,000,000. Owing to the increased business last fall and winter they have been building another plant which is now completed at a cost of about $2,500,000. Whereas in 1930, when hon. gentlemen opposite were in power, they were employing 1,000 people, they are now employing about 1,500, and with the new addition to the plant they will be employing in a few weeks' time about 2,000. In other words, there will have been an increase in employment in that one industry alone in four years of one hundred per cent.
We have another new industry, the Powdrell and Alexander concern, which is a branch of a large American firm manufacturing materials used in the making of window shades. They are employing 200 people working full time. That industry came to Cornwall because of exceptional advantages the town offered, but it first had to decide to come into Canada, and it did so because of the tariff policy of the present government. Then there are three cotton mills which found it necessary two months ago to put on a night shift in one of the mills and to take on 130 additional people. In conversation with representatives of the clothing industry, I have been informed that this business has been better in the past few months than for some time previously. The manufacturers of metal beds, of which there is an industry in Cornwall, have also benefited by the policy of the government. We have two paper mills which manufacture fine book paper used in the publication of magazines. They have tried to point out that he was bleeding the people of western Canada, forgetting all the time that

The policy of the present government has, since it has been put into effect, assisted very materially the textile industry in the county which I represent. That industry is one of the oldest in Canada. First there was wool, then the manufacture of cotton, later on the manufacture of silk and during the last few years the synthetic product, rayon. The first cotton mill was established at Sherbrooke, Quebec, in 1844; the second at Thorold, Ontario, in 1847. I note in the budget which has been brought down there is a reduction of one and one-half per cent in the excise tax on British imports; which is am additional sacrifice that will have to be made by Canadian manufacturers. I am firmly in favour of the Canadian textile manufacturer and every other manufacturer getting the protection to which they are entitled, and I speak more particularly on behalf not only of the manufacturer himself, although he deserves credit, but also of the thousands of men and women who are employed in these industries and for whom the policy of the present government has done so much to enable them to obtain regular employment and decent wages.
The official opposition have continuously attacked the manufacturing industries of Canada. I wish to draw their attention to the fact that according to the census returns there were in 1931, of those ten years of age and over gainfully employed in the manufacturing industries of Canada, 442,759 men and women. Yet bon. gentlemen opposite continue to maintain that these industries are receiving too much protection, that in fact they are not

entitled to so much consideration. There was a time when voices were raised from the liberal benches on behalf of the manufacturing industries of Canada. I can recall years ago when there were men from both Ontario and Quebec who did not sit so quietly and listen to their colleagues attack the manufacturing industries; knowing as they did their importance in the economic life of Canada they were always ready to rise to their defence. Sir Lomer Gouin, one of Canada's great men from Quebec in the years gone by, more than once defended the industries of Canada. Prior to my time in the house I remember reading speeches of the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), who comes from an industrial section of Ontario, and who was ready to rise in defence of the industries of Ontario and Quebec. But those voices are silent now; there is no one in the Liberal opposition to defend these industries which are so important in our industrial life. I want to ask hon. gentlemen opposite a question. Their leader has told us-I have quoted this before, you will find it on pages 263-4 of Hansard for the fall session of 1932-that if he were returned

The Budget-Mr. MacMillan (Mackenzie)
to power one of his first acts would be to restore the Liberal tariff as it was when they went out of office and increase the British preference to an average of fifty per cent of the general tariff. What would happen to the industries of eastern Canada if that policy were put into effect? I know what would happen in my constituency; at least 1,500 people would be thrown out of work inside of six months or a year. I want to ask hon. gentlemen opposite what they propose to do for these men and women that they would throw out of employment. Are they going to take them out to the wheat fields of western Canada to grow more wheat to add to our already large surplus?
The policy of the party now in power, the policy of this government, is a truly national policy which aims to help all sections of Canada, and I believe in that policy. I believe that Nova Scotia coal and fish from the maritime province should be used by the Canadian people to the largest possible extent. I believe we should use all the beet sugar we possibly can to give aid to the beet sugar industry. I have bought and sold many thousands of pounds of beet sugar in my time, and I was glad to do it because I looked upon it as a one hundred per cent Canadian product. I believe we should give a preference to white sailors in British Columbia rather than to foreigners. But I also believe that the industries in my part of the country should receive the same consideration from hon. gentlemen from other parts of the country that I am willing to accord to theirs.
I think it can be safely said that Canada is coming through this depression as well as if not better than any other country. I attribute that to three reasons. The first is the character of the Canadian people. Coming from the great parent races, British and French, reinforced by the very best which the nations of Europe had to offer, our fathers were a pioneer stock and they have transmitted to the Canadians of to-day those pioneer characteristics of courage, determination and energy and the will to overcome difficulties which I believe have been great factors in helping our people through these trying times. The second reason is the abundant natural resources which we possess, greater I think than those entrusted to any other nation of ten million people in the world. The third reason, and just as important as the other two, is the fact that we have been singularly fortunate in having at the head of affairs in Canada during these difficult years a statesman who is the epitome of all the best characteristics which the Canadian people
possess, that in the Prime Minister of Canada we have one who demonstrates in his life these characteristics of determination, the will to succeed, the ability to overcome difficulties, the greatest heritage that our pioneer forefathers have handed down to us. I believe also we are fortunate in that in his cabinet he has surrounded himself with a group of men of the same type, men who during these trying years have been devoted to the interests of the Canadian people. An article by Isaac F. Marcosson published in a January issue of the Saturday Evening Post, entitled "North of the N.R.A.," has often been quoted before, but I would like to direct the attention of the house to it, because it is an article that every Canadian should read. The writer is a disinterested and trained observer who has spent many years in travelling and studying the conditions in various countries and has fitted himself to form a clear and accurate judgment of those conditions and the reasons why they exist. In that article he gives a very high place to Canada among the nations of the world for the way in which she has survived the difficulties by which she has been beset, and he gives the reasons I have enumerated, namely, the character of the Canadian people, our abundant natural resources, and the fact that we have been fortunate in having at the head of affairs a statesman and government who have devoted their very great abilities to the best interests of our country.
