But the bank would not take it. They did however, write their loan down from $700 to $500 and brought sufficient pressure on him to have this sale. When the sale was over it did not bring in $700 or even $500; it brought $241.05.
I give these figures because I think it is essential that the people in this part of Canada should know the extraordinary situation that the farmer on the prairie is struggling against. I am glad to learn from the Minister of Finance that the government intends to bring in a bill designed to liquidate to a certain extent the farmers' debts, or the expression used I think was to enable them to stay on the land. I cannot say much with regard to the legislation proposed, as we have not particulars, except that I am glad it is coming. But I want to warn the government right now that it will have to foe much more far-reaching than the long term farm loan act of a few years ago. That has given very little relief indeed. I shall withhold further comment until the legislation comes down, but I hope when it does come I shall be able heartily to congratulate the government on what they propose. Then I understand the government intends to bring in a bill with regard to public works. I hope that it will include provision for finishing those branch lines of railway where the grade has been prepared already but the rails are still wanting. I have in my mind one particular grade running some twenty^five miles easterly from Bulwark. The grade is all ready, it only awaits the steel, and completion of this line is very urgently needed. The farmers there have been waiting for many years, living a long distance from elevators and putting up with a great deal of hardship. I sincerely hope that when the public works program comes down such undertakings will be considered. I have taken the matter up with the Minister of Railways several times, and I hope we shall now see provision made for finishing such public works.
In conclusion I should like to refer to some of the defects in our economic system as I see them. Our problem is not one of unemployment, but of unpurchasable production;
that is, that people are unable to buy the goods which they want and which are already made. This brings about consequent unemployment, with the usual glut of goods; production thereby is further reduced, and there is the consequent poverty. Poverty is caused not by unemployment but by lack of purchasing power accompanied by economic need. We have many people who might be called unemployed, but they are spoken of as leisured because they have money to spend. We have, as outlined so ably by the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon, industrial plant much greater than we really need, although we could use it a good deal more if the people were able to purchase the goods that can so readily be made. This brings about frantic cut-throat competition in selling goods, because of the vast amount to be sold and the few who are able to buy and the many who can buy but little. This defect in the means of selling goods brings about the next stage, the grabbing for foreign markets. As each country is trying to do the same thing we are drifting into worse and worse economic warfare which undoubtedly will lead ultimately to military warfare. It seems to me, therefore, that instead of spending so much time and money and consideration in an attempt to find markets abroad for our surplus products, we should pay more attention to satisfying the needs of our own people. I was reading, the other day a most interesting book on the life of Napoleon, and I noticed that he considered that the problem that should engage his attention first of all was that of agriculture, next industry, and third external trade. Canada would do well if she followed a similar line of reasoning.
As I have said, the problem of every country to-day is how to get rid of goods, and they are trying to get rid of them by export. But we have a real demand at home, and our problem is to turn that real demand into effective demand. If we have not money sufficient to buy the goods that are made, that is allowing for the exchange of goods between export and import, we have not the money to buy the goods that come into this country in exchange for the exports. A glut of goods, as we well know, means that factories shut down, more and more men are out of work, with consequent lack of purchasing power and increased burden of taxation on those who are working in order to take care of those who are unemployed. So it seems to me that we have to pay more attention to the matter of purchasing power. In these
The Budget-Mr. Butcher

times agriculture is the industry that feels the distress most because it is least organized, consequently the prices of agricultural products drop first and are usually the last to recover. Therefore the responsibility of government at this time is to enable the farmer to get a fair return for his work, which will have the effect of bringing about an improvement in all industry.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand it to be the custom, when taking part in the budget debate, to refer to matters that have been alluded to by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) in his address, and I understand also that it is the privilege of horn, members who have some other subject much in mind to speak upon that subject. I propose to avail myself of that privilege this evening. Before doing so, however, I should like to congratulate the Minister of Finance upon the manner in which he delivered his budget address. I could not help sympathizing with him as to some of the material contained in that address, though I must admit that there was some occasion for rejoicing in connection with other parts of his speech.
To-night I want to speak upon a subject to which I referred early in February, that is, the need for the amendment of our company laws. A little later in the session the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) said he thought possibly the amendments proposed in the speech from the throne would not be proceeded with this session, but at a still later date the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) stated that a new companies act would be brought in, and I understand that this new act has been brought in and is now upon the members' files. I want to congratulate the government, and particularly the Secretary of State, for their action in bringing down this bill this session. I have not had time to study the act as yet, but if it is as stringent as the Secretary of State suggests I am sure it will meet with the approval of this house. In his preliminary remarks the hon. gentleman said:
The bill also contains very strict and stringent provisions with regard to the issue of prospectuses by companies or by underwriters on behalf of companies.
Later he said:
They are so much more strict and stringent than the provisions of the provincial companies acts that if this act is adopted I think it may result in a very serious diminution in revenue for the consolidated fund, because until provincial acts are amended or modified in like manner many applicants for charters certainly will go to the provincial authorities rather than to the dominion authority.

I congratulate the Secretary of State upon this disregard for the consolidated revenue fund. I think it is very fortunate that the government has decided, regardless of the loss of revenue, to improve our companies act and make it less possible than it has been in the past for fraudulent companies to operate. The minister concluded his preliminary remarks by saying:
*-I trust this bill will receive the careful consideration of hon. members of the house before it is dealt with by the committee of the whole.
I am confident that this is precisely the reception that will be accorded this bill.
As I said just now, Mr. Speaker, early in February I referred to certain matters in connection with the promotion of companies in the Dominion of Canada during the last few years. I prefaced my remarks by saying that undoubtedly the majority of the promotions had been of a strictly honest character but that there had been many that were decidely dishonest, and that there had been dishonest promoters of companies who had defrauded the public without mercy. I then went on to speak of financiers and financial organizations that had promoted mergers and combines in Canada that were illegal in some cases and near illegal in others, that were distinctly detrimental to the interests of the public and positively disastrous to investors. I said further that these questionable and in many cases immoral ventures frequently were connected with the necessaries of life, such as bread, milk, fruit, fish, coal, textiles, pulp and paper, asbestos and cement. I omitted to say "among others" as I had intended, but I think it was clear to the house that I was not trying in the least to make grave disclosures at that time. I was not trying to inform this house of the conditions that existed, because I knew that the majority of hon. *members were perhaps better informed than I was. I was trying to remind this house once again that the time was ripe for an improvement in our company laws in order to prevent a recurrence of the disastrous happenings of the past ten years in the matter of company finance. Nor was I trying to attribute blame to any government, either federal or provincial, either past or present; I was trying to draw attention to certain evils and to suggest certain remedies. The day following my speech the Prime Minister made this remark in the house:
There are thousands of men and women in Canada to-day who have been practically

The Budget-Mr. Butcher
ruined because of the shares they bought in various enterprises in this country during the last seven years. It is a blot upon this country's financial history.
So I had the Prime Minister with me in the opinions I expressed the previous evening. I am informed that on the following day one of the Montreal papers said, "Everybody knows these things." I did not see that statement personally, but if it be true that everyone knows these things certainly it is equally true that it is the duty of someone or some authority to do what may be possible to prevent their recurrence. It seems to me every hon. member of this house has to line himself up either with the reformers on one hand, those who believe in preventing that kind of thing in the future, or on the other hand with those who say that the law of the jungle is the right law, who believe in the survival not of the fittest but of the slickest, as the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) said some time ago; who believe that it is every man for himself, and his Satanic majesty take the hindmost. It may appear to some hon. members that I am suggesting locking the stable after the horse has been stolen. Admittedly horses have been stolen but, to pursue the metaphor further, there are still horses in the stable and there will be others later on, so surely it is advisable now to provide the bars, the locks and padlocks that will prevent further thefts.
On reflection it seemed to me that when I spoke on February 1, I said too much or too little in regard to certain necessaries of life that had been the subject of the operation of wrongful combines and mergers. I had said that in the case of combines and mergers, monopolies or near monopolies had been created, and by practical monopoly of purchasing power the price to the producer had been forced down; by oppression of labour wages had been forced down, and the pace had been speeded up to a point almost beyond endurance; that by virtual control of output prices had been raised and the consumer had been gouged. I agree with what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said this afternoon with regard to the benefits or lack of benefits resulting from many of these mergers and combines. I am unable to see that they have benefited in any way the producer, the consumer or the investor, or that they have proved of greater benefit to labour than the smaller, independent units. The question then arises: Have they benefited anyone and, if so, whom have .they benefited? They have benefited the promoter only.
First I am going to refer to milk, which was the subject of an inquiry by the agriculture and colonization committee of this house last session, when much interesting information was brought to light. I do not think I need refer to the result of that investigation, because every hon. member had the opportunity of following the proceedings of the committee from day to day, but I do want to give in brief the history of just one company, tracing it from its very inception to the present time, in order to prove that there has been an evil in connection with the formation of companies to deal with this much needed commodity.
I am going to quote from several newspaper articles to prove my point. In the Financial Times of October 15, 1926, there appeared the photograph of a certain gentleman who was described at the foot of it as the "originator of many utility and food enterprises in Canada." The article went on to say that he had just completed the purchase of National Food Milk Products Limited. Previous to this it is understood that he had been fifteen years in Alberta, during which time he had originated two large utility enterprises. Then he came to eastern Canada and "saw the possibilities for development in food product lines." He is not the only one who has seen the possibilities for development in food product lines. Unfortunately there have been too many of them.
This gentleman, having come upon a very promising little dairying industry in or near the town of Gananoque in the province of Ontario, conceived the idea of forming a company to handle this little dairy, and the National Milk Products Limited was formed.
This preliminary notice of October 15, 1926, was followed by another a week later in the Monetary Times under the title of "New Company Issues." It was stated that this new company was being floated with a new issue of $150,000 six and one-half per cent twenty year first mortgage sinking fund gold bonds.
Then we leave National Milk Products, Limited and we find in the Produce News of November 30, 1928, an announcement of the formation of another company called the Canada Dairies, Limited, which we are told was a consolidation of seven Toronto dairies.
Four months later, on March 18, 1929, we are told that Canada Dairies, Limited, has acquired the company which I first mentioned, National Milk Products, Limited. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that the securities of
The Budget-Mr. Butcher

National Milk Products were placed on the market on October 22, 1926. I should have said that at that time first mortgage bonds for S150,000 were outstanding, and $150,000 of preferred stock.
In the Financial Post of December 26,
1929,	just nine months after Canada Dairies, Limited, had acquired National Milk Products, Limited, we read:
National Milk has gone into receivership. It is not known how much the bondholders will receive.
I think, sir, it might have added:	It is
definitely known how much the preferred shareholders will receive-they will receive nothing.
We find that:
National Milk was a subsidiary of Canada Dairies, Limited, but the latter company did not guarantee the $150,000 of bonds outstanding . . . and had cut loose from the Gananoque firm, leaving whatever can be got from it for the bondholders.
That is a very casual statement. What did it mean for the poor bondholders and shareholders? I am informed, and I believe credibly informed, that the people of the town of Gananoque contributed 1250,000 in the purchase of the securities of this company. These people in the town and the farmers in the concessions to the north and the south, the east and the west, including probably many a poor labouring man, contributed their little quota for the purchase of a share of that company. A very casual statement-"whatever could be got was left for the bondholders.''
In the Financial Times of December 16,
1930,	we read that a special meeting of Canada Dairies, Limited was held to confirm, "if deemed advisable, by-law authorizing sale of assets of Canada Dairies, Limited to the Dairy Corporation of Canada, Limited."
On June 4, 1932, we read that Canada Dairies put on a customer-ownership sale, offering $50,000 six per cent first mortgage bonds to pay off old mortgages, assisted by the Dairy Corporation of Canada. The public is invited to carry this load. We read from that very article as follows:
The original company consisted of a merger of six or seven small companies arranged by-
I shall not give the name:
-and other associates not now associated with the business.
It is a remarkable fact that whenever these companies get into trouble, those who are responsible for their formation are found to be "not now associated with the business." They have got away with their profits, leaving

the people who put up the money to bear the loss. The article goes on to say:
About $800,000 was paid for these concerns but in the upshot a large part of the business was lost in merging and results were unsatisfactory.
Those who bought about $300,000 in preferred stock have not found their investment satisfactory.
Again, a very casual way to put itl Men who have lost $300,000 would hardly regard their loss as merely unsatisfactory. Most of them would think of other words which are far more appropriate, if less polite. Who lost that $300,000? What labour does it represent? What distress does the loss of it entail?
But there is still left the Dairy Corporation of Canada, and what of it? It consists of a merger, and what do we hear of this company recently? We read that it had to be reorganized, that in 1930 the company had issued sinking fund debentures to the tune of one million dollars, which were "secured by first floating charge on all company's assets and undertakings. Company cannot mortgage, pledge, lien or charge upon the mortgaged premises," and so on. But we are informed that there was a joker in the trust indenture, that these debentures were never a first lien, that they were always "subject to the bank loans and other secured charges in the ordinary course of business." In a circular letter accompanying particulars of the new scheme of reorganization, the president of the company sententiously remarks, "The payment of this bank loan is a problem." The only comment one can make on that is: What wisdom!
One of the subsidiary companies of the Dairy Corporation of Canada was the City Dairy of Winnipeg. It may be that hon. gentlemen have recently been receiving a little magazine called Wilton's Review from Winnipeg. It contains very interesting information with regard to this company known as City Dairy. My reason for referring to these companies is that I want to point to certain evils that exist in the constitution of many of our companies to-day, and at the same time to point out possible remedies.
On February 17 of this year a meeting of the shareholders of City Dairy was held. At this meeting it was disclosed that when the shareholders bought their preferred stock only 4,500 preferred shares were authorized; that the preferred stock became entitled to voting power after one year's default; that 2,000 of these preferred shares participated with the common stock in dividends over seven per cent and up to ten per cent; that at that time

The Budget-Mr. Butcher
there were 3,000 shares of the common stock of a par value of $100 in existence; that in 1933 all the preferred stock being in default as to dividends the holders naturally thought that they controlled 4,500 votes as against the 3,000 votes in common stock. But they were mistaken. They discovered that the 3,000 shares of common stock of the par value of $100 had been converted into 15,000 non^par shares, and thus that they had lost control.
How had this happened? In 1930 certain by-laws designed by the holders to place the common stock in a permanently dominant position were duly passed, and in course of time a petition for supplementary letters patent was filed in the office of the provincial secretary. The facts recited in the petition were apparently quite truthful and very frank. On September 27, 1930, supplementary letters patent were granted. In an article which appeared in the Financial Post of March 17, 1934, the president of the Dairy Corporation of Canada is quoted as follows:
In 1930 the capital structure of City Dairy was changed and gave the Dairy Corporation of Canada sufficient common shares to outvote the preference shares if those preference shares assumed to vote owing to dividends being in arrears.
A scheme of rearrangement was submitted, and what happened? Those who contributed $450,000 will be absolutely at the mercy of the holders of the original 3,000 common shares, who did not pay more than $100 per share. I know that this particular case is no business of the federal government, but it' illustrates what is quite common in the formation of companies. I hope this is an evil which is being dealt with in the amendments to the Companies Act.
I referred to bread, and I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) referred to the same subject this afternoon. I should like to give a few facts with regard to this commodity. In 1931, the allegation having been made that several bread companies had formed an illegal combine, an investigation was held, either by the registrar under the Combines Investigation Act or by a commissioner. During the course of his investigation the registrar found that four milling companies operating bakeries had then acquired ninety-six bakeries in Canada. They manufactured one-third of all the bread manufactured in Canada and ninety per cent of the bread manufactured in the communities in which they operated. Taking these facts in conjunction with those given this afternoon by the minister the house will see the control which could be exercised by these four milling companies operating bakeries throughout Can-74726-170
ada. The house will realize how easy it would be for price agreements to be made by these four companies. At the conclusion of his report the registrar states:
No conclusive evidence has been adduced to show that this combination constitutes a combine within the meaning of the Combines Investigation Act. At the same time, the predominant position of these flour milling companies in the baking industry, and the possibilities of monopoly and price enhancement which are theirs, are such as to warrant continued governmental interest in the situation, and, should the need arise, further governmental action on behalf of the consuming public.
It is quite evident that these four companies have something which very nearly approaches a monopoly of the bread business in eastern Canada. The very idea of monoply is repugnant to the free thinking people of Canada. Men who seek to control any industry are never actuated by altruistic motives but are invariably themselves controlled by a ruthless lust for power and financial gain. Have these combinations benefited the consumer in any way? Have they benefited the producer in any way? Have they benefited the labourer or have they benefited the investor? Poor's appraisal of the securities of these milk and bread companies to which I have referred is, with one exception, "speculative" or "very speculative."
I referred to coal but I do not propose to speak on that matter this evening. I understand that the decision of the court as to the existence of an illegal combine has been appealed and I shall make no further reference to the matter.
I referred to fruit also. It is within the memory of hon. members of this house that in 1926 four companies and four individuals were fined $200,000 in all because they had formed an illegal combine in fruit. Although I have not the facts, I believe there is a general impression that a similar combine exists to-day.
I mentioned fish also. I might point out that recently an inquiry was held in Manitoba into an alleged combine in connection with the fishing industry of that province. The commission found as follows:
We have found that a combination exists between four companies and that other companies have agreed with them, to regulate and control a large proportion of the summer caught fish on lake Winnipeg.
Time will not permit my going into details with regard to this alleged combine in fish.
I referred to asbestos. I do not believe I have time to deal further with this except to say that the inquiry recently held or at

The Budget-Mr. Butcher

present being held in the United States goes to show that the control of asbestos is almost world wide and that J. P. Morgan and Company have presumably acquired control not only of Canadian companies but of companies in Great Britain, Europe and on the north American continent. The Prime Minister, speaking recently, I believe in Toronto, referred to the asbestos situation in Quebec and the desire of the president of that company to purchase asbestos in Russia rather than in Quebec.
I do not think it is necessary for me to amplify the remarks I made on February 1 in connection with cement. In 1909 there were 11 chief producers who had been brought together at a cost of $14,822,250. Stocks and bonds to the tune of $27,134,786, or almost twice the cost of purchase, were issued. Even with this huge capitalization satisfactory dividends were paid. However, in 1927, Wood, Gundy and Company and associates purchased this company and recapitalized at $35,000,000, although it was alleged that there had not been any corresponding increase in capital assets. Despite the water in the stock satisfactory dividends were paid. But in 1923 a cloud appeared upon the horizon which seemed disastrous to this large company. The National Cement Company was incorporated, but this was a competitor not to be endured. In 1928 the National Cement Company was acquired by Alfred Rogers and associates and in 1929, a year later, Canada Cement took over National Cement. We now have practically a monopoly in cement products which are used for thousands of purposes by practically every industry in Canada. Again I ask: Has this huge monopoly benefited the consumer? Have the labourer and the investor been benefited? Poor's appraisal of this particular stock is " speculative."
I referred to pulp and paper, but as my time is going rapidly I do not think I can deal with this matter except to say that the history of the Canada Paper and Power Corporation is one of greed and mismanagement of finance. I should like to make two quotations. I made one in this house about two years ago, and the other is contained in a letter which was addressed recently by a firm of investment bankers to I believe practically every member of parliament. Mr. Taschereau is quoted as having said that in 1920 there were 100 paper mills, producing $100,000,000 a year in products, capitalized at $22,000,000, employing 31,000 employees, and paying them yearly $45,000,000. At the end of ten years there were 109 mills, producing $215,000,000

in products, but capitalized at $714,000,000. There had been an increase of 2,000 in employees but payrolls remained the same as in 1920. While production increased by 115 per cent, capitalization increased by 3,500 per cent, roughly speaking. I quote from the letter of the investment bankers as follows:
In general, the financial and industrial leadership in Canada has differed only in degree from the depredations of the robber barons of medieval Europe, the brigands of Tartary or other ungodly countries, the Corsairs of Algeria or the pirates of Penzance.
This firm of investment bankers stated that the above was an extract from a published article by the president of a well known Canadian life insurance company. Again I ask: Did this combination benefit labour? Did it benefit the producer or the investor? If not, whom did it benefit? It benefited the promoters only.
I was going to refer to Dominion Textiles, but time will not permit.
Having dwelt for a few minutes on these mergers and combines, the operations of which have been distinctly detrimental to the interests of the people of Canada, I wish to refer now to some fraudulent company promotions through which investors have lost millions. Possibly hon. members are wondering why I did not leave these remarks until the second reading of the new Companies Act, but I wanted to speak with greater latitude than probably I should have been permitted to do had I waited until that occasion, when one would be expected to speak only on the principle of the bill. In every one of these instances I propose to point out an evil and suggest the remedy. Take the O. J. Brooks ventures, which resulted in the loss of from [DOT]ten to twelve million dollars to the people of Canada. This man Brooks came to Canada in 1921 and promoted seven finance corporations and finally promoted Brooks Steam Motors Limited. He took from the people of Canada, as I say, from ten to twelve million dollars, including about $3,800,000 in Brooks Steam Motors alone. How was this accomplished? It was accomplished by the illegal use of common stock and no par shares. I had hoped to be able to deal at considerable length with this particular company but time will not permit. Suffice it to say that I will point the moral before closing my remarks. There is another company to which I wish to make some reference and that is a concern referred to in an editorial of the Free Press of Winnipeg of May 18, 1928. This was a western company owned by a famous westerner, Senator Patrick Burns, and a small

The Budget-Mr. Butcher
group of associates. This company had a prosperous record and looked like a good thing. I have looked up the prospectus as well as the Toronto Globe of May 18, 1928, and I find that the prospectus was issued by the Dominion Securities Corporation Limited, on May 16, 1928. On May 12, 1928, this company, the Dominion Securities *Corporation, had addressed a letter to the shareholders then in the concern, reading in part as follows:
We have purchased the business of P. Burns & Company Limited. There will be a rearrangement of the capital structure which will necessitate calling for redemption the 6J per cent first mortgage bonds at 104 and accrued interest on the first of Juy next, and a formal notice of this call has already appeared in the press.
Notwithstanding this letter, dated May 12, 19(28, the company issued a prospectus four days later stating:
From the letter of Mr. John Burns, to be president of the company, we summarize as follows:
The prospectus concludes thus:
These statements have been accepted by us as accurate, but are in no event to be construed as representations by us.
This prospectus makes very alluring statements to show that the earnings of the company are far more than sufficient to pay interest on all securities offered for sale. But in a letter recently issued by the Preferred Shareholders' Protective Committee some very strong statements are made, and I suggest to hon. members that they take the first opportunity of reading this communication. I am quite satisfied that they will agree that an investigation should be made into the affairs of this company and into the history of its capitalization. Again time forbids that I should deal in detail with the operations of this particular company.
Now I wish to point out briefly the lessons to be learned from these cases. National Milk Products illustrates the need of closer supervision of promotions and especially of those promoters who are so ready to "see the possibilities of development in food product lines" and in public utilities.
City Dairy Limited illustrates the evil of the "abstraction of the vote" to which I should like to refer, but I am afraid I shall be unable to do so; I hope to have the opportunity on the second reading of the Companies Act. It also teaches the evil of the no par value share.
The case of the mill owned bakeries shows that concentration of the production of any food line is detrimental to the interests of the 74726-170 i
public, and that our present concept of what constitutes an illegal combine needs some adjustment.
The case of the Dairy Corporation of Canada seems to show that there should be some official charged with the responsibility of bringing those responsible for withholding necessary information to the bar of justice; for what is the business of many people usually becomes the business of none. And trust companies who have undertaken to protect certain classes of shareholders should not be able to evade all responsibility for fulfilling the trust by employing the customary formulae but should be held responsible to those shareholders in every case in which there is a "joker" in the trust deed.
The tobacco inquiry, the fish combine in Manitoba and the asbestos case illustrate the need of a widening of the legal interpretation of what constitutes an illegal combine.
The cement case illustrates the need of a stricter control of the capitalization of mergers and so forth, and similarly the pulp and paper situation.
The textile situation suggests that the time has arrived for limitation of the earning capacity of mere money capital.
The Brooks ventures illustrate the evil of bonus stock, call it stock watering or illusory capitalization, whichever you will, and the necessity of our courts passing upon the adequacy of the consideration given for shares, when called upon to do so. There are other cases to which I wish to refer but I am afraid I shall have to postpone consideration of them.
The case of Burns and Company Limited suggests that the person or corporation issuing a prospectus should not be able to hide behind the formulae usually employed but should be held directly responsible for all statements contained therein. A casual glance over the new Companies Act shows however that provision of that kind has already been made. And all the cases combined seem to suggest the necessity of the erection of an investment board clothed with large powers of investigation and control.
There are many other matters which I should like to have dealt with but I shall speak of them when the bill is before the house.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is customary for members of parliament speaking on the budget to refer to the wonderful manner in which the minister of finance presents it to the country. I (believe that in the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) Canada is blessed, as it has been in
The Budget-Mr. Bradette

times past, with a man. highly qualified for the office, and the way in which the hon. gentleman presented the budget now before the house was a credit not only to himself but to parliament. But in bringing down the budget he must have found himself in a very embarrassing position for more than one reason, one of the main reasons being the rash promises made on previous occasions by his party and his government, and also by reason of some of the principles and policies enunciated by outstanding members of the government when they were in opposition. These were brought forcibly to the attention of the house by the opposition financial critic, the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston).
One thing in particular which the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) advocated and which made a strong impression at the time was the turnover tax. It is not my intention to deal at any length with this but merely to refresh the memory of the house, pointing out how easy it is to propound new policies if not new fallacies which are very workable in opposition but difficult of application when men are in responsible positions of government. The same thing applies to the statement of the Prime Minister that if he were in power he would almost compel the insurance companies of this country to take up the national debt at a lower rate of interest than then prevailed. Several other theories were propounded by the then opposition and in each case when they have the responsibility of administering the affairs of the country, they find those theories impossible of application. I recall very vividly that time after time not only in this country but throughout the civilized world new parties, fads and fallacies come out which look well at the time but when those parties take on the responsibility of government, they also find their ideas impossible of application for the simple reason that they would be detrimental to the country as a whole.
One matter I want to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance is the fact that last year parliament through legislation reduced the interest rates on savings accounts by one per cent. But one thing that will strike every hon. member is the fact that if anybody wants to get a loan from any of these banks which have received special treatment from parliament, no doubt on account of the fact that savings were coming in too rapidly for the demand made on the banks because of the high rates of interest charged by them, he cannot borrow at a lower rate of interest. In my section of the country prior to last year when we wanted to borrow any money from the banks, the rate of interest was eight 
per cent, and this compounded at least four times a year. We find ourselves in the same situation this year. Why is it that when the reduction in the interest rate on savings accounts was granted to the banks the interest rate on loans made to their customers was not also regulated so that loans might be at a lower rate than we have to pay at the present time? If the banks are overloaded with savings deposits they can find an outlet for their money in good solid investments whether in industry or all kinds of new commercial enterprises or the refinancing of the older institutions.
I should like now to allude to something which I have already mentioned in the House of Commons: I refer to the refinancing of the Canadian National Railways. I believe the day is now at hand when that refinancing should be done so that the people, the owners of the system, may know exactly where they stand in regard to the financial structure of that great institution. We know the propaganda that has been spread against national ownership of our railways, and it is not fair, when we are discussing that all-importani matter, not to mention the fact that our national railway system has been overloaded with dead timber, dead material and dead capitalization, all of which it has absolutely no right to be shouldered with the responsibility of financing at this time.
I want to mention briefly a regional aspect which greatly affects our section of the country. I have mentioned this on several occasions and I wish to repeat it. So far as the section of the Transcontinental from Quebec to Winnipeg is concerned, it has never come into its own because it has never received the attention of the present or past governments in regard to the through traffic, freight or passenger, to which it is entitled. I well remember twelve or fourteen years ago the great rejoicing we had throughout northern Quebec and northern Ontario when the first through passenger and freight service was established; I well remember the demonstration made by every section of that part of the country. But the story was much sadder when over a year ago the passenger service was entirely done away with so far as through transportation from Quebec city directly to Winnipeg was concerned. Those fine national trains, numbers one, two, three and four, without warning to our section, were entirely withdrawn, and to-day there is no possibility of travelling directly from Montreal or Quebec or the maritime provinces to Winnipeg. The situation is worse because of the fact that since those two trains were cancelled practically all

The Budget-Mr. Bmdette
the traffic is lost to the Canadian Pacific. I speak of this question with knowledge; I know the people in my section find it impossible to travel directly between Winnipeg and Quebec city. When we want to go to Winnipeg, we have to come around by North Bay. In my section where we have a population of over 100,000 I do not think since the curtailment of that passenger service five per cent of the people who go to the west travel Canadian National. That accounts somewhat for the problem facing the Canadian National and explains certain loss of revenue. Why that service was ever curtailed I have never been able to learn either from the government or from the railway 'board. It is possible even at the present time to reestablish that sendee so as to allow the Canadian National to come into its own. Everybody who is familiar with the old line of the Canadian Northern where the traffic is now routed, knows that it goes through practically a wilderness; it does not go through a settled country such as we have in northern Ontario. I say to the house, and particularly to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) so that he may use his influence, that the passenger traffic should be reestablished over the northern section of our country, if not to Cochrane through North Bay over the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway, at least from Montreal to Harvey junction and from there to Winnipeg. In that case so far as the through traffic is concerned, the railway would come into its own. That section has suffered on account of lack of service and the Canadian National has suffered by losing that revenue to the Canadian Pacific without any benefit to the people.
I want to felicitate the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) on his wonderful speech, and I feel all the more at liberty to do so because it was recognized as such even by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) when he spoke this afternoon. Not only was the hon. member speaking as a financial critic but he was propounding suggestions that will help the present government if they try to implement them. People from all sections spoke well of his ability in discussing matters of such great' national importance.
I want to concentrate my remarks particularly on a subject in which the whole country is interested: I refer to the gold tax. I am quite at liberty to speak on it because I do not own either directly or indirectly any stock of any mining corporation in any section of this country, and I have no interest whatever in the gold mining industry. Moreover, I can speak with an open mind on the matter because our section, when any problems, local or regional or national in character, arise, always tries to take the viewpoint of the whole of Canada. If one part of this country is affected by this tax we feel that the whole of Canada will be affected. I was . astonished this afternoon when the Minister of Trade and Commerce tried, I believe, to insinuate that the protest that was made in the house against the tax was merely a local one. The gold mining industry of Canada to-day affects every citizen, and although its activities are centred in only three or four provinces, the beneficial effects are experienced throughout the whole dominion. The Minister of Trade and Commerce knows well that in my section hundreds of carloads of lumber coming from British Columbia are being used every year in the Porcupine district alone. The gold mining industry affects every economic and industrial activity of our country and therefore the question is not parochial; it is one that affects every section.
Let me go further. The gold mining industry realize that they have duties towards the country as they have towards the province and the districts in which they are situated; therefore the industry is willing to bear its proper and reasonable share of federal taxation. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) is not here, which I regret, as I would like to have some further light on some statements he made on that matter. He said, on April 23, as reported on page 2446 of Hansard:
The financial critic of the opposition has suggested that this tax means a discrimination against a particular industry. Well, I would point out that that is true of all our indirect taxation.
I do not see how that statement will bear the light of analysis, because we are actually singling out one industry under the present system of taxation. There are other industries, which I am going to mention later on, that have been making large profits during the past year. Take for instance Imperial Tobacco; their annual report shows they made last year a profit of about six million dollars, but we have not applied a special tax on that exorbitant profit. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre goes on to say:
Our whole tariff schedule means that particular industries are singled out for taxation, so there is nothing new in that contention.
The Budget-Mr. Bradette

As far as I know, tariffs are not taxes on industry but are in fact intended to help and shelter industry. Take the oil or the textile industries: Imperial Oil, for instance, had a net profit of nearly twenty million dollars last year, but there is no proposal in the present budget to tax that particular industry, which is not being taxed by the tariff but is being sheltered and helped by artificial protection.
He goes further:
Further than that, it is suggested that it is discrimination against particular parts of the country.
As with the human body, if one section of the country suffers distress, then the whole country suffers. Although geographically we belong to central Canada, we have never taken a parochial attitude with regard to maritime rights, for instance, or the fruit growers of British Columbia or other activities of our national life. This is not a local problem; it is entirely a national problem. You cannot call the gold mining industry a local industry, because its beneficial effects are felt in every channel of our national life. Then the hon. gentleman says also:
Further it is suggested that the budget does not take into account the variations in the grades of ore and costs of production.
Doubtless the Minister of Finance in the very near future will come out with a statement corroborating what has been said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is an anomaly to put a flat tax of ten per cent on gold produced regardless of profits. I intend to show how low grade ores are being treated, and how thousands of men will be thrown out of employment if that tax is applied uniformly to all the gold mines. I believe I am right in saying that the Flin Flon is working on ores yielding an average of $2,70 per ton on which they make a clear profit of IS cents per ton. Any hon. member can easily visualize what will happen as a result of this tax to mines operating on such low grade ore. The Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon gave us a ray of hope in suggesting that some amendment of the taxation proposals in that regard will be made. It will have to be made, otherwise the government will find very quickly that instead of being beneficial the tax will work its own destruction. It will throw out of employment a lot of men and paralyze to a large extent many sections of our country.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre went on to say:
I do not believe it is common that such variations should be taken into account.

He certainly showed a very sad lack of knowledge in leading the house to believe that the gold mines are working on a definite ratio of actual gold per ton. I shall in a few minutes name mines that are worldng on an average gold content of $2.75 and similar figures, and others where the veins are so narrow that more rock has to be mined than ore; so that the hon. member, posing as a friend of the worker, showed a sad lack of understanding. I believe he was in the town of Timmins last year, where he would see one mine alone, the Hollinger, that employs 2,800 miners. It had a chance under the new price of gold of increasing its capacity by working *lower grade ore than in previous years. Then the hon. member went on to say:
If we did fully take them into account it would be a bonusing of the marginal mines.
Well, it may surprise hon. members to know that out of 475 mines actually in operation at the present time there are about 15 on a dividend paying basis. Can you visualize, in view of that, what harm may be done by a flat taxation of ten per cent of all production? Then he went on to say:
Since this enormous gain in the value of gold is entirely a fortuitous gain-
That is a very fine word to use. Are not all gains in commerce and industry fortuitous? This afternoon another hon. member, also a labour leader, for whom I have great respect, asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce what amount of money was spent in subsidies for gold mining. I may tell the hon. member that the government of Canada has not given a single cent of subsidy to our gold mines. The government practically seized the gold produced. If it had been allowed to go for instance to the New York market the mines would have received the very same price as was paid by the government. The government simply paid the price that the gold producers would have received in the New York market.
Then the hon. member went on:
Of course, some one will say that would mean that certain mines would not be able to gain as much as they are doing to-day, that certain lower grade mines would be discriminated against, that a certain number of men would be turned out of work, and so on. I know there may be all these objections, but they apply equally in any taxation of this kind, because a good many industries have been put out of business through the very high taxation placed upon them in the purchase of the raw materials required for their products.
Again that is a statement which astonished me, because I do not know of any taxation

Dominion Elections Act
or tariff restrictions against any raw material coming into this country. I know of no tariff for instance, on raw rubber or raw cotton coming into Canada.
Then the hon. member spoke of the nationalization of our gold mines. I wish he were here, because I was going to ask him what mines he would nationalize. Would he nationalize only the paying mines, the fifteen that are on a dividend paying basis, or every gold mine in operation at the present time?
I notice, Mr. Speaker, that there is not a single member of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group in his seat at the present moment, although time and time again they have been complaining of the lack of attendance of members of the two other parties.
On motion of Mr. Bradette, the debate was adjourned.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, May 1, 1934
